question: This school reunited with its former junior college in 2009, bringing their secondary and pre-university sections under one administration. Its crest features a gryphon, and its school colours are green, black and white. Its Latin motto, Auspicium Melioris Aevi, expresses hope for a better age. Founded in 1823, it traces its origins to the British official who established Singapore as a trading settlement. For 10 points, name this Singapore school named after that colonial founder.

The clock tower on this school’s campus became a national monument in 1999, preserving a landmark of its predecessor. Its present form dates to a 2005 merger between a secondary school and its affiliated junior college. That junior college had opened in 1974, while the secondary school traced its founding to Tan Kah Kee in 1919. The secondary predecessor was known in English as The Chinese High School. For 10 points, name this Singapore school whose two-word name is often followed by “Institution”.

The nature reserve sharing this peak’s name is connected to the Central Catchment Nature Reserve by the wildlife crossing called Eco-Link@BKE. Its forest includes a surviving patch of primary rainforest, preserving vegetation that predates the surrounding city’s development. Visitors follow hiking trails through that reserve to reach its summit. Despite its national prominence, this summit rises only a little over 160 metres above sea level. For 10 points, name this elevation that forms Singapore’s highest natural peak.

This interjection was among the Singapore English additions to the Oxford English Dictionary in March 2016. Speakers often place it at the beginning of a sentence to announce a reaction to something they have just noticed. It can convey admiration or delighted surprise, depending on the surrounding words and delivery. For 10 points, give this one-syllable Singlish exclamation spelled with three letters, beginning with W and ending with H.

Completed in 2009, this shopping centre was developed by Lendlease as part of Singapore’s established retail district. Its retail space occupies eight levels, providing several floors of shops and places to eat. Visitors can enter it directly from an MRT station below, without first returning to street level. The mall stands along Orchard Road, within Singapore’s main shopping district. For 10 points, name this mall whose branded name starts with a three-digit palindrome and includes an at-sign.

Kameron Saunders used a version of this expression on the fifth night of Taylor Swift’s Singapore concerts in March 2024. That version ends with the additional discourse particle, a form also discussed in academic writing about Singlish. The phrase can convey irritation or surprise, and a linguistic analysis glosses it as “Oh my god”. Its second syllable ends in an “ng” sound, distinguishing it from another common exclamation ending in “lao”. For 10 points, give this two-word Singlish outburst of shock or exasperation.

The village of Kampong San Teng grew around a burial ground on land that later became this residential town. That burial ground was known as Peck San Theng, and the town’s name derives from the Mandarin pronunciation of part of that name. Redevelopment transformed the former cemetery landscape into a housing estate. Today, Junction 8 serves shoppers here beside the town’s namesake MRT interchange. For 10 points, name this Singapore town whose name is associated with the old cemetery’s “jade hills”.

This body of water was once called the Impounding Reservoir and later carried the name Thomson Road Reservoir. In 1922, it received its present name in honour of a municipal engineer associated with its expansion. Boardwalks along its edges allow visitors to explore the forest while following the shoreline. Completed in 1868, it marked an early step in developing a public water supply for the island. For 10 points, name Singapore’s first reservoir, which bears the surname of that engineer.

A famous statue of this creature suffered a lightning strike in 2009 that damaged its mane and sent debris falling to its base. The same statue had been moved to a new site near One Fullerton in 2002. The completion of Esplanade Bridge had obstructed views of it from the waterfront at its earlier location. Its fish body recalls Singapore’s fishing-village origins, while its head evokes the city’s name. For 10 points, name this mythical Singapore icon combining a fish with a lion.

This attraction spans the gap between Bukit Peirce and Bukit Kalang, giving visitors a view into the forest canopy. From its elevated crossing, hikers can look out towards the waters of Upper Peirce Reservoir. Its deck reaches about 25 metres above the forest floor at its highest point, well above the ground-level trails. The crossing itself measures approximately 250 metres from end to end. For 10 points, name this freestanding suspension bridge in Singapore’s Central Catchment Nature Reserve.
answer: TreeTop Walk [or Tree Top Walk; or HSBC TreeTop Walk]

question: This politician earned a master’s degree in economics at the London School of Economics after graduating from the National University of Singapore. Before becoming a minister, she served as an assistant secretary-general of the National Trades Union Congress. She first entered Parliament in 2006, beginning a political career that later included several ministerial portfolios. She led the Manpower Ministry from 2018 to 2021, including during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic. For 10 points, name this Singaporean woman who subsequently took charge of the communications and information portfolio.

The basement of this bungalow hosted political meetings in 1954, before the People’s Action Party became Singapore’s governing party. The Lee family had moved into the property after the Second World War. Decades later, a provision requesting its demolition became central to a public disagreement among the family’s children. Its best-known resident remained here until his death in 2015. For 10 points, give the house number and street of this longtime home of Singapore’s first prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew.
answer: 38 Oxley Road [or 38 Oxley; or thirty eight Oxley Road; prompt on Oxley Road]
